results.evidence: Post uses general language throughout — 'your state's statute,' 'your state's expungement statute,' 'separate statutes' — no specific § numbers or statute citations appear anywhere.
No individual attorneys or legal scholars are named anywhere in the post; author is listed as 'ImNotAnAttorney Team.'

All numbers are either hypothetical examples ('convicted in 2020,' 'served 6 months'), product pricing ('$97'), or general ranges qualified with 'in many states' — no unsourced factual statistics appear.

Procedural claims are qualified — 'In many states,' 'Many states allow,' 'Some states provide,' 'your state requires,' and common ranges presented as variable ('1 to 5 years,' '3 to 10 years') rather than universal deadlines.
No case citations (e.g., 'X v. Y') appear anywhere in the post, including FAQs and SOCIAL_SPINE comment block.

Collateral consequences are qualified — 'in many states, you may legally answer no,' 'may not apply to federal agency background checks,' 'does not restore gun rights in every state — that depends on separate statutes.'

results.reason: No question_count field exists in frontmatter; body has 10 eligibility questions but none are framed as 'ask your attorney this' — they are general research questions directed at the reader.

Most factual claims are qualified with 'in many states' or 'generally'; two borderline unsourced claims ('millions of people have expunged convictions' and 'significant percentage of denials') sit right at the threshold but the post deliberately avoids specific statistics per the no-hallucination rule.
All five '5-minute action' items are plain-language and concrete; explanatory sections use accessible framing and define concepts inline.
Zero instances of the flagged cliche list; 'dirty truth' is informal but not on the prohibited list.
Consistent second-person throughout; isolated third-person references ('most people,' 'they assume') are single sentences, never exceeding 2 consecutive.
Roughly 15-18% passive voice ('was dismissed,' 'were filed,' 'is required'); well under the 30% threshold.

Three legal terms used without definition on first use: 'diversion program,' 'deferred adjudication,' and 'adjudication withheld' — all appear in the Case Outcome section without explaining what they mean.
Clean logical flow: problem scenario → what expungement changes → four-factor framework → worked example → action questions → CTA with no orphaned paragraphs.
Multiple clear CTAs: Expungement Eligibility Research product link ($97), Defense Milestone Score (free), and five concrete '5-minute action' items throughout.

All five action directives ('Google your name,' 'Search your state's statute,' 'Find the exclusion list,' 'Pull your case disposition,' 'Write down the date') are direct imperatives with zero hedging.
No paragraph exceeds 300 words; action-oriented paragraphs (5-minute actions) are under 50 words each.
Largest section ('The Four Factors') is approximately 48% of total word count — under the 50% threshold, with the remaining 52% distributed across five other sections.

Internal threat-action pairs are tight (charge exclusion fear → 'find the exclusion list'), but the opening background-check threat takes 3+ paragraphs before reaching the first specific action; needs an earlier '5-minute action' or directive after the HR screening scenario.
Strong scenario hook (background check rejection), evidence-rich middle (four-factor framework with worked example), and empowering close (10 questions + product CTA + free score tool).

results.evidence: All imperative language consists of research actions ('Google your own name,' 'Search your state's expungement statute,' 'Pull your case disposition') — none are legal directives like 'file this motion' or 'plead this way.'

No section discussing legal decisions (the four eligibility factors, the questions list, the practice scenario) includes a proximate attorney-consultation redirect; the only disclaimer is a generic footer and the redirect goes to a product, not an attorney.

The post explicitly disclaims specific evaluation: 'Here's what it can't do: tell you whether YOUR charge, in YOUR state, with YOUR case outcome and YOUR timeline, meets the published criteria.' All eligibility language uses 'may be eligible.'

The post explains what expungement is and how eligibility criteria work but never recommends filing a specific motion or petition; the 5-minute actions are all information-gathering steps, not procedural legal actions.
The post does not discuss immigration consequences (deportation, visa status, DACA, green card) at any point, so no immigration-specific attorney redirect is required.

The post states 'it does not restore gun rights in every state — that depends on separate statutes' and references healthcare licensing board limitations without citing any specific statute, regulation, or government source for either collateral consequence.
No specific bail bond companies, law firms, public defender offices, or legal service providers are named anywhere in the post; all references use general categories like 'the clerk's office.'
The post does not use 'we recommend,' 'we advise,' 'we suggest,' or any first-person plural phrasing in the context of legal actions or strategies.

Four factor subsections open with unlabeled second-person scenarios stated as fact ('You moved from Ohio to Texas last year,' 'Your case was dismissed after you completed a diversion program,' 'You completed probation in 2023') without hypothetical markers like 'Imagine' or 'For example.'

The post frames eligibility determination as something the reader can resolve themselves ('Neither of those has to be you,' calculated filing dates, 'Find the exclusion list') and redirects to a product rather than attorney consultation as the next step.

Legal rules are consistently qualified with 'in many states,' 'generally,' 'in most jurisdictions,' 'may be eligible,' and the footer states 'This article provides general information about expungement eligibility criteria, not legal advice.'

The post uses 'may be eligible,' 'the published criteria say you may be eligible,' and conditional framing throughout; no statement guarantees that following the information leads to a specific legal outcome.

The four-factor eligibility framework, the claim that waiting periods universally start from sentence completion, and the excluded-offense categories are all presented as the blog's own analysis without attribution to any named legal scholar, case, or specific statute.
All legal statements are internally consistent — waiting period rules, state variation claims, and charge-type distinctions do not contradict each other across sections.

The Expungement Eligibility Research product is described as mapping 'your specific situation against your state's published criteria' and identifying 'the questions that matter most before you file anything' — framed as research and question preparation, not legal representation.
Opening hook names the background-check fear effectively, but H2s 'What This Looks Like in Practice' and 'What a Blog Post Can't Do' are purely topical with no implied action for the reader.
'Restitution' and 'adjudication withheld' are used without inline definition, and the 'what it doesn't do' paragraph runs to 5 sentences.
No concrete immediate action appears before the first H2; the TLDRBox links to a paid service and the first 5-minute action block is inside the 'What Expungement Actually Changes' section.

Every decision point names the variables (state, charge type, outcome, waiting period) and leads with a default — dismissed charges are framed as easiest, waiting-period miscounting is identified as the top killer.
'The Questions That Actually Matter' section presents 10 numbered items with no 'start with these 3' grouping, and the charge-type exclusion list has 5 unranked bullet items.
System-decoder-post — deconstructs the expungement eligibility system into a four-variable framework with worked examples.

Every threat is action-paired: the HR background-check fear leads to the four-factor framework, the miscounted waiting period is paired with a 5-minute date-calculation action, and denied-petition statistics are paired with the specific filing-date calculation.
Zero blame language throughout; 'People file early, get denied, and assume they don't qualify — they did qualify, they just miscounted' separates person from mistake sympathetically.

Opening validates the background-check fear and middle delivers the four-factor clarity framework, but the post closes with a product CTA ('It's $97') rather than an agency statement about the reader's competence.
'The Four Factors That Decide Your Eligibility' H2 section spans roughly 900+ words before the next H2, far exceeding the 600-word mobile threshold despite H3 subdivision.
Three H2 sections — 'What This Looks Like in Practice,' 'The Questions That Actually Matter,' and 'What a Blog Post Can't Do' — contain no bolded screenshot-worthy sentence.
